source.title: The 10 Hardest Math Problems That Remain Unsolved

accepted.question_text: For the function f defined on natural numbers by f(n)=n/2 when n is even and f(n)=3n+1 when n is odd, does iterating f from every natural number always eventually reach 1? In other words, starting from any natural number and repeatedly applying the rule "halve if even, otherwise triple and add 1", is it true that every resulting trajectory eventually lands on 1?

evidence.quote: Take any natural number, apply f, then apply f again and again. You eventually land on 1, for every number we’ve ever checked. The Conjecture is that this is true for all natural numbers.
while the story of Tao’s breakthrough is good news, the problem isn’t fully solved.

accepted.question_text: Is every even integer greater than 2 expressible as the sum of two prime numbers? A proof must establish this for all even integers, not only for the many cases verified computationally.

evidence.quote: Goldbach’s Conjecture is, "Every even number (greater than two) is the sum of two primes."
Computers have checked the Conjecture for numbers up to some magnitude. But we need proof for all natural numbers.

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many pairs of prime numbers that differ by 2? Equivalently, do twin primes occur infinitely often among the prime numbers?

evidence.quote: When two primes have a difference of 2, they’re called twin primes.
So, are there infinitely many twin primes? The Twin Prime Conjecture says yes.

accepted.question_text: Do all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have real part 1/2? That is, whenever the zeta function is zero at a nontrivial complex input, must that zero lie on the vertical line in the complex plane whose real part equals 1/2?

evidence.quote: the official statement is, "Every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2."
Today’s mathematicians would probably agree that the Riemann Hypothesis is the most significant open problem in all of math.

accepted.question_text: For equal spheres in Euclidean space of dimension greater than 3, what is the maximum possible number of spheres that can simultaneously touch a single sphere? More generally, is there a complete general solution or formula for the kissing number as a function of the dimension?

evidence.quote: When a bunch of spheres are packed in some region, each sphere has a Kissing Number, which is the number of other spheres it’s touching
Beyond 3 dimensions, the Kissing Problem is mostly unsolved.
For larger numbers, or a general form, the problem is wide open.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an algorithm that can determine whether any given knot can be untangled to the unknot in polynomial time? If not, can one instead prove that no such polynomial-time algorithm is possible, so that the computational difficulty of unknot recognition is inherently greater than polynomial time?

evidence.quote: Where the Unknotting Problem remains is computational. In technical terms, it’s known that the Unknotting Problem is in NP, while we don’t know if it’s in P.

If someone comes up with an algorithm that can unknot any knot in what’s called polynomial time, that will put the Unknotting Problem fully to rest. On the flip side, someone could prove that isn’t possible

accepted.question_text: Is the real number π+e algebraic or transcendental? More generally, for simple combinations of the two known transcendental constants π and e, such as π+e and π/e, can one determine whether the resulting number is algebraic or transcendental?

evidence.quote: But somehow it’s unknown whether π+e is algebraic or transcendental.
Similarly, we don’t know about πe, π/e, and other simple combinations of them.

accepted.question_text: Is the Euler-Mascheroni constant γ a rational number? Equivalently, can γ be written in the form p/q for integers p and q, or must it be irrational?

evidence.quote: But somehow, we don’t even know if γ is rational.
We’ve calculated it to half a trillion digits, yet nobody can prove if it’s rational or not.

needs_review.question_text_raw: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture is another of the six unsolved Millennium Prize Problems... Its exact statement is very technical, and has evolved over the years.

evidence.quote: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture is another of the six unsolved Millennium Prize Problems
Its exact statement is very technical, and has evolved over the years.

needs_review.question_text_raw: In some senses, the top of the large cardinal hierarchy is in sight... But many open questions remain... Hopefully we’ll eventually have a comprehensive list of all large cardinals.

evidence.quote: But many open questions remain, and new cardinals have been nailed down as recently as 2019.
Hopefully we’ll eventually have a comprehensive list of all large cardinals.
